be59ed81d79044cb5ec49d5a3ee86cc12d5a5221.message:
fix(security): keep the SPA CSRF cookie alive across authenticated responses

With stateless auth the default CsrfAuthenticationStrategy treats every
authenticated request as a fresh login and clears the XSRF cookie on each
response; plain JSON endpoints never re-render the deferred token, so the
browser loses it and the first write after login dies with 403 and a
forced logout. Swap in NullAuthenticatedSessionStrategy — rotation stays
with CsrfTokenRotator on login/logout — and re-bootstrap the token from
the SPA right after both transitions. SpaCsrfBrowserFlowTest replays the
real browser sequence (bootstrap → login with the old token → read →
first write), which the MockMvc csrf() post-processor cannot catch. The
vite proxy target is now overridable via VITE_PROXY_TARGET so the dev
walkthrough can point at a local backend, and the cross-layer contract is
pinned in .trellis/spec/backend/security-guidelines.md.

e1cc78321d5fe3ce1f12b402d3f43fee2a66ea73.message:
fix(deploy): give every response the security headers only the edge can add

The SPA and the API went to browsers with no CSP, no nosniff, no
referrer or permissions policy - any successful XSS had free rein, and
the response never said otherwise. These headers can only be set
credibly at the edge proxy, because that is the one hop every response
shares.

nginx now sends a locked-down set at server level: CSP allows scripts
from self only, styles from self plus Google Fonts (with
'unsafe-inline' because Vue :style bindings become style attributes),
fonts from gstatic, connections from self only, and no frame embedding
in either direction. X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options,
Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy back that up for older
behaviours, server_tokens stops advertising the nginx version, and HSTS
ships inert - browsers only honour it over HTTPS, so it costs nothing
today and starts working the day TLS terminates in front.

Two nginx subtleties are load-bearing. add_header is inherited as an
all-or-nothing group, so the headers live at server level and no
location adds its own. And every header uses `always`, otherwise 4xx
and 5xx responses - exactly the ones an attacker probes - would go out
bare.

The SSE stream for the agent timeline gets its own location: proxy
buffering held events inside nginx until timeout, which silently
degraded the UI to its polling fallback, and the default 60s read
timeout would have cut every quiet stream and caused a reconnect storm.

deploy/test-nginx-headers.sh boots a throwaway nginx with this exact
config and asserts all headers on a 404 response (proving `always` at
the same time), without needing the compose stack. Verified passing
locally; a follow-up commit wires it into CI.

2eaf008cdbc2ca4ac6828abb065e2ff9571caaba.message:
feat(csrf): give the SPA real CSRF protection behind the frozen switch

The API authenticates with a cookie, and browsers attach cookies to
cross-site requests on their own. Any page could therefore submit a
state-changing request on behalf of a logged-in user; SameSite=Lax
narrows the window but does not close it for top-level POST navigations.
There was no second factor tying a write to our own frontend.

This lands the standard SPA recipe by hand, because CsrfConfigurer.spa()
does not exist in Spring Security 6.5.7: the token travels in a
non-HttpOnly XSRF-TOKEN cookie and comes back in the X-XSRF-TOKEN
header. SpaCsrfTokenRequestHandler is the one subtle piece - tokens are
issued XOR-masked so a token rendered into a compressed response cannot
feed BREACH, but the header value is the raw token read straight from
the cookie, so it must be compared raw. Mixing those two up rejects
every legitimate request.

GET /api/auth/csrf is a public bootstrap endpoint: calling it
materialises the cookie and returns only the cookie and header names,
never the token value. Login rotates the token, because the pre-login
token may have been planted in the victim's browser by the attacker
(session fixation applied to CSRF); logout deletes it. Webhooks are
exempt - GitHub cannot know our token - but the test pins down that
exemption from CSRF is not exemption from signature verification: a bad
signature still gets 401.

The switch stays app.security.csrf.enabled=false, per the frozen
cross-track contract: flipping it on is a merge-time act, and the other
track's tests do not send tokens yet. The suite runs almost entirely
with the switch off, which is exactly the regression evidence that the
default-off deployment keeps working. 6 tests cover bootstrap, missing

fbb2ea7e7f6189d0b7c8aef4dc8586827e1d100d.message:
feat(audit): give security-relevant actions one recognisable event stream

Security actions left almost no usable trace. A failed login was a 400 and nothing else, so no one could tell a typo from someone working through a password list. Rotating a webhook secret or a write-back credential was completely silent. An authorization denial was a 403 status code that reached no log at all, because Spring Security produces it before any controller runs. Answering "who did what to which object, and did it succeed" meant reconstructing it from unrelated business logs.

SecurityAuditLogger writes one fixed key=value line per event to a dedicated security.audit logger, carrying action, outcome, actor, resource, client, trace and reason. Successes are INFO, failures and denials WARN so they survive the default level. Nothing sensitive is admitted: no tokens, cookies, passwords, webhook secrets, patch bodies or payloads, and reason takes a caller-supplied stable code rather than an exception message, which can carry internal paths. Field values are sanitised because the actor name is attacker-controlled - a newline in a username would otherwise let someone append a forged "outcome=SUCCESS" record of their own. The client IP is stored as a 12-hex HMAC keyed with the application secret, which correlates events from one source without keeping addresses in the log.

Login now distinguishes lockout, unknown user, bad password and disabled account in the audit stream while the HTTP response stays deliberately uniform - the enumeration defence is about what the caller sees, not what the operator can read. Credential rotation on an SCM installation records which installation changed and whether the write-back credential was replaced, never the values. Webhook deliveries record the two rejection paths, unknown installation and failed verification.

The rest is covered by a filter rather than by touching every controller: it sits outside the security chain, so it observes the final status and catches denials the business code never sees. It records writes, 403s, rate limiting, and 401s that presented a credential - an anonymous 401 happens on every page load before login and would drown the signal. Reads are not recorded. Login, logout and webhooks are skipped there since they emit their own, more precise events. 16 tests cover the format, the redaction, the digest and each filter rule.

57b77861774b80942f49b372da42717eee254a46.message:
fix(webhook): verify before recording, and make delivery idempotency atomic

The webhook endpoints are reachable by anyone, yet they persisted a delivery row before establishing that the caller held the shared secret. Two consequences followed. An attacker could probe delivery ids and read back the agent run id of a real delivery from the DUPLICATE acknowledgement, and any unsigned request left an audit row behind, so the table could be filled at will. Both endpoints now resolve the installation and verify the signature over the raw bytes first; unverified traffic is logged and dropped without touching the database, and the acknowledgement carries no run id.

Idempotency was also check-then-write, which is not idempotent under concurrency: two simultaneous copies of the same delivery both miss the lookup, both insert, and one dies on the unique key as a 500. The new WebhookDeliveryRecorder, shared by the two controllers, instead attempts the insert and treats a unique-key violation as proof that another request already claimed it, re-reading that row to answer DUPLICATE. The existing uq_scm_delivery_provider_delivery constraint carries this, so no migration is needed. Finally the raw payload is no longer stored: it can carry branch names and commit messages, and only a hash plus metadata is retained unless a debug flag is set.

ec67e35a2d40a53bd7dc6d6a788e26f2b430cefe.message:
fix(git): drain git output off-thread and block SSRF-capable repo URLs

Two defects on the outbound git path. First, run() called waitFor before reading the pipe, so any command whose output exceeded the OS pipe buffer (~64KB) deadlocked: git blocked writing, we blocked waiting, and the command died at the 60s timeout. Log and diff on a real repository exceed that routinely. Drain stdout on a daemon thread started before the wait, capped so an outsized diff cannot exhaust the heap, and keep reading past the cap so the child never stalls. The failure message also carried git's raw output, which can echo an inline-credential remote URL or the askpass helper path, so redact the token, the helper path and user:pass@ forms before it reaches the API or logs.

Second, repository URLs were only checked for scheme and shell-injection, so binding http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ or http://127.0.0.1:8080/actuator made the server clone its own network. Add OutboundUrlPolicy, applied to every http(s) repo URL: it rejects loopback, private, link-local, unique-local, CGNAT and reserved ranges across all resolved records, plus DNS-independent hostnames like localhost/.local/.internal. Non-standard numeric forms (0x7f000001, 017700000001, 2130706433) are refused outright rather than resolved, because git goes through glibc inet_aton and Java's parser disagrees, so a Java-side verdict would not describe the address actually dialled. An unresolvable host is not treated as hostile - doing so would let a DNS blip reject legitimate repositories.

9a964f24963e6f0545ba4cf48b86127870fc609b.message:
fix(knowledge): persist failed indexing state and bound upload input

Upload ran embedding and vector indexing inside one transaction that
marked the document FAILED and then rethrew. The rollback discarded the
status change along with the document row, so a failed upload left no
trace at all: the caller saw a 500 and the document list stayed empty,
with nothing recorded about what had been attempted or why. A slow
embedding provider also held a database connection for its whole run.

Upload is now three phases. The document row is created and committed on
its own, indexing runs with no transaction open, and the outcome is
written by a REQUIRES_NEW transaction that survives the caller unwinding.
The stored reason is sanitised so provider URLs and raw exception text do
not reach a column the API returns.

Input is bounded before any of that. Uploads were accepted on the
strength of a .md or .txt suffix, then read whole into memory with
getBytes() and decoded leniently, so a binary blob named notes.md became
a stream of replacement characters and got chunked, embedded and indexed.
Reads are now capped and streamed, NUL bytes are rejected, decoding is
strict UTF-8, and blank or over-long text is refused. Filenames are
reduced to a sanitised basename before storage.

Indexing takes the committed entity rather than reloading it by id: the
call is read-only, and status changes still reload inside their own
transaction, so nothing writes back through a detached entity.

a4ca72002065d22f066efedb47b739d5f9006bf4.message:
refactor(agent-step): split claim, execute and completion; add heartbeat lease

Step execution was one @Transactional method that also took a pessimistic
row lock, then called the handler inside it. Every Git clone, model call,
sandbox run and SCM write-back therefore held a database connection and a

had already had external side effects.

Execution is now three phases. A short transaction checks the attempt
rules and stamps an execution token; the handler runs with no transaction
open at all; a second short transaction records the result only if this
worker still holds the token. A worker whose lease was reclaimed mid-flight
now has its result discarded instead of overwriting whoever took over.
Completing a step and enqueueing the next one stay in one transaction, so
a run cannot succeed a step without scheduling its successor.

The lease is renewed by a heartbeat rather than being a fixed window. A
fixed lease forces a bad trade: long enough for the slowest step and a
crashed worker strands the run that long, short enough to recover quickly
and the watchdog starts killing steps that are merely slow. Renewal makes
an unrenewed lease a real liveness signal, which the recovery queries now
consult before interrupting anything.

Recovery also runs periodically, not only at startup — a worker that dies
while the process stays up used to leave its step RUNNING until the next
restart.

Scheduling for both background loops is consolidated behind one flag,
default off so test contexts get no background threads racing their
assertions, and on in prod.

9be72b35f46fe14ed2a1f9df0d2e26549fe58de1.message:
fix(agent-outbox): add scheduler, claim lease and terminal failure

The outbox had no production driver at all: publishAvailable was only
ever called from tests, and @EnableScheduling did not exist anywhere in
the application. An Agent run enqueued its first event and stopped, so
the core pipeline never advanced on its own.

Three defects are fixed together because each one masks the next.

A scheduler now drains the outbox, reclaiming expired leases before each
publish pass. @EnableScheduling sits on the scheduler class rather than a
global config so that test contexts, which leave the flag off, get no
scheduling infrastructure and no background writes racing their
assertions. The flag defaults to off and prod turns it on.

Claims carry a token and a lease. Publishing happens with no transaction
open, so a worker can lose its claim mid-flight; every write-back is now
conditional on (id, claim_token, PROCESSING), which makes a late worker's
result update zero rows instead of clobbering whoever reclaimed the
event. A reaper requeues leases that ran out, incrementing the attempt
count so a worker crashing in a loop still converges.

SENT now means the broker said so. Publisher confirms and returns are
enabled in prod, and an event is only marked sent once a confirm arrives
without a return; nacks, returns and confirm timeouts all go back to
PENDING. Delivery is at-least-once by construction, so consumers must
stay idempotent. Retries are bounded by max-attempts and exhausted events
move to a terminal FAILED state instead of being republished forever.
